summary: Updates the iCalendar and vCard formats, RFC 5545 and RFC 6350, so that parameter values can include certain characters the earlier specifications forbade. It does this through an escaping mechanism for those characters.

plainLanguage.summary: Calendar and contact files carry extra information on the same line as a field, in a part called a parameter. This RFC defines a short escape sequence so that a parameter value can contain a double quote or a line break without breaking the file.

subtitle: A way to put double quotes and line breaks inside iCalendar and vCard parameter values.

tldr.problem: The syntax of iCalendar and vCard forbids double quotes and control characters inside a parameter value, but extensions keep needing to put them there. The backslash escape used for property values is not defined for parameters and cannot be reused.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the caret as an escape character in parameter values. A line break becomes ^n, a caret becomes ^^, and a double quote becomes a caret followed by a single quote.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard published in February 2013 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 5545, RFC 6321, RFC 6350 and RFC 6351, and the new sequences are safe for old parsers because the escape never contains a double quote.

facts.label: Line break escape
facts.value: ^n, a caret followed by the letter n

facts.label: Double-quote escape
facts.value: ^', a caret followed by a single quote

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: Parameter values whose type uses the param-value syntax element

facts.label: Unknown escape
facts.value: A caret followed by any other character is left in place along with that character

today: RFC 6868 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2013, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 5545, RFC 6321, RFC 6350 and RFC 6351 so that parameter values can carry double quotes and line breaks, and it deliberately keeps the new escape sequences free of double quotes so that parsers written before it still read the file correctly.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The iCalendar specification of RFC 5545 defines a standard way to describe calendar data, and the vCard specification of RFC 6350 defines a standard way to describe contact data. Both use a similar text-based data format. Each iCalendar and vCard data object can include properties that have parameters and a value. The value of a parameter is typically a token or URI value, but a generic text value is also allowed.

The syntax rules for both formats prevent the use of a double-quote character or control characters in such values, though double-quote characters and some subset of control characters are allowed in the actual property values.

As more and more extensions are developed for these data formats, there is a need to allow at least double quotes and line feeds in parameter values. The backslash-escaping mechanism used for property text values is not defined for use with parameter values and cannot be easily used in a backward-compatible manner. This specification defines a new character escaping mechanism, compatible with existing parsers and chosen to minimize any impact on existing data.
sections.plainLanguage: A property line looks like a name, then some extra words in brackets that qualify it, then the value itself. The extra words could not contain a quote or a line break. Extensions need to put those in, so a way of writing them is needed.

sections.title: The Parameter Value Encoding Scheme
sections.content:
The specification defines the caret character, U+005E, as an escape character in parameter values whose value type is defined using the param-value syntax element, which is Section 3.1 of RFC 5545 and Section 3.3 of RFC 6350. The escaping mechanism can be used whether the value is unquoted or quoted, that is, whether or not the value is surrounded by double quotes.

When generating parameter values, a formatted text line break is encoded into the two characters ^n, the caret and the letter n. The caret character itself is encoded into ^^. The double-quote character is encoded into ^', a caret followed by a single quote.

When parsing parameter values, the sequence ^n is decoded into an appropriate formatted line break according to the type of system being used. The sequence ^^ is decoded into the caret character. The sequence ^' is decoded into the double-quote character. If a caret is followed by any character other than those, parsers must leave both the caret and the following character in place.

When converting between the iCalendar and vCard text-based data formats and alternative representations such as XML, as described in RFC 6321 and RFC 6351, implementations must ensure that parameter value escape sequences are generated correctly in the text-based format and are decoded when the parameter values appear in the alternate formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Three sequences to learn: a caret and n for a line break, two carets for a literal caret, and a caret and an apostrophe for a double quote. A caret followed by anything else is left exactly as it is, so a stray caret does not corrupt the value.

sections.title: Examples in iCalendar and vCard
sections.content:
The first example is an ATTENDEE property with a CN parameter whose value includes two double-quote characters. The parameter value is not quoted, because there are no characters in the value that would trigger quoting as required by iCalendar:

The unescaped parameter value is the text George Herman "Babe" Ruth.

The second example is a GEO property with an X-ADDRESS parameter whose value includes several line feed characters. The parameter value is quoted, because it contains a comma, which triggers quoting as required by vCard:

The unescaped parameter value, where each line is terminated by a line break character sequence, is the three lines Pittsburgh Pirates, 115 Federal St, and Pittsburgh, PA 15212.
sections.plainLanguage: The first example puts a nickname in double quotes inside the display name of an attendee. The second example puts a three-line street address inside a quoted parameter, using the escape sequence for the line breaks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: There are no additional security issues beyond those of iCalendar in RFC 5545 and vCard in RFC 6350.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new. The security rules of the two formats it changes apply unchanged.

sections.title: Choice of the Escaping Mechanism
sections.content:
The appendix of the RFC explains why the caret was chosen, and why the backslash was not.

Adopting the backslash escaping used for property values was the obvious first choice, but it could not be used as it stands, because it escapes a double quote as a backslash followed by a double quote. The Section 3.1 example would then look like this. Existing iCalendar and vCard parsers know nothing about escape sequences in parameters, so they would parse the parameter value as the text between the first and second occurrence of a double quote, that is, the text up to the backslash. The text after the second double quote ought to be a colon or a semicolon, to delimit the parameter value from the following parameter or property, but it is not, so the parser could legitimately throw an error at that point because the data is syntactically invalid. For backward-compatibility reasons a double quote cannot be escaped using a sequence that itself includes a double quote, and hence the choice of using a single quote in this specification.

Another option would have been a form of backslash escaping modified for use in parameter values only. However, some incorrect, non-interoperable use of the backslash in parameter values has been observed, so it is best to steer clear of it to achieve guaranteed, reliable interoperability. Also, because the double quote changes to a single quote in the escape sequence for a parameter but not for a value, it is better not to give the impression that the same escape mechanism, and thus the same code, can be used for both. That impression could lead to other issues, such as an implementation incorrectly escaping a semicolon as a backslash-semicolon instead of quoting the parameter value.

The choice of the caret as the escape character was made on the requirement that an ASCII symbol, a non-alphanumeric character, be used, and that it be one least likely to be found in existing data.
sections.plainLanguage: The backslash was rejected for a concrete reason: the old escape for a quote would itself contain a quote, and a parser that does not know about escapes would then stop at the wrong place and reject the file. The caret was picked because it is unlikely to appear in real data already.

viz.caption: Why the backslash was not used for parameter values

cells: Backslash escaping as used for property values

It escapes a double quote as a backslash followed by a double quote. A parser that knows nothing about escapes would stop at the wrong double quote and then hit a syntax error, because the text after it is not a colon or a semicolon.
A modified backslash escaping for parameters only
Incorrect, non-interoperable use of the backslash in parameter values has been observed, and a separate mechanism risks the impression that one piece of code can escape both parameters and values.
An ASCII symbol that is least likely to be found in existing data.
